problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =5:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$

Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd  one). So, the rank of $A-5I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-5I) & =3-\text{rank}(A-5I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A-5I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
